lead: Wilmington sits between the Cape Fear River and the Atlantic. Hurricane Florence cut the city off in 2018, and heavy rain and humidity still drive most of its water damage.
risk: hurricane flooding, heavy rain and mold
why: Hurricane Florence came ashore near Wrightsville Beach in September 2018 and stalled for days. Wilmington got more than 20 inches of rain, and floodwater closed every major road into the city for a time. Trees fell on roofs across town, and power was out for days. Water came into homes from rising creeks and through damaged roofs.

Smaller storms still cause trouble. Heavy summer rain can overwhelm drainage in low parts of Midtown and near Burnt Mill and Hewletts creeks. Many Wilmington homes have crawl spaces, and the humid coastal air keeps them damp. A small leak there can turn into rot and mold. Fewer than half of homes are owner-occupied, so many leaks involve renters and landlords.
image_alt: Roofer in a harness on a roof under tall trees
image_caption: After Florence, many Wilmington homes needed roof repairs before drying could even start.
problems: Low areas near Burnt Mill and Hewletts creeks
Oak-lined streets in Forest Hills, Carolina Heights
Older homes downtown and in Brooklyn
Crawl space drying and mold control
tips: Know your evacuation zone and your home's flood risk.
Buy flood insurance early; it usually takes 30 days to start.
Add a vapor barrier and keep crawl space vents working.
Renters: report leaks in writing and take photos right away.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, Carolina Heights, Forest Hills, Sunset Park, Brooklyn, Midtown, Mayfaire and Pine Valley, plus Wrightsville Beach, Leland and Carolina Beach.

faq.q: Who pays for water damage in a Wilmington rental?
faq.a: It depends on the cause. The landlord's policy usually covers the building, and the landlord handles leaks from pipes, roofs and appliances they own. A renter's policy covers your own belongings. Report the leak in writing, take photos and move items away from the water.
